q: Placing two elements side by side so their differences stand out by comparison — what design term names this?
o: Positioning elements close together or side by side, especially to compare or contrast them, so each one's distinct qualities stand out against its neighbor
Judging an object's size against some familiar reference point
Mixing different elements together to keep a space visually interesting and avoid monotony
Emphasizing importance through relative size, shape, or placement
n: Juxtaposition is the state of being placed close together or side-by-side, especially for comparison or contrast. In architecture, it is used to highlight the unique qualities of individual elements by showing how they differ from their neighbors.

q: Ceiling-mounted fixtures that light a whole room evenly belong to which artificial-light category?
o: Natural Light
Task Light
Accent Light
Ambient Light
n: Ambient Light provides general illumination, such as ceiling lights.

q: Alternation, as a rhythm device (think black-and-white tiles or a striped fabric), is best defined as what?
o: Gradual changes in elements
The use of the same color across a space
A subtle, smooth flow from one space to another
Two or more elements alternating in sequence, such as black and white tiles or striped fabric
n: Alternation is two or more elements alternating in sequence — e.g., black and white tiles or striped fabric.

q: Complete the definition: the Golden Section is ___
o: A mathematical ratio found in nature, thought to be inherently pleasing to the human eye, expressed when a line is divided such that the ratio of the whole to the larger part is the same as the larger part to the smaller part
The ratios of a musical scale applied to the dimensions of rooms
A 20th-century scale of proportions based on a man with an arm raised
A vernacular modular system based on a floor mat
n: The Golden Section is a mathematical ratio found in nature, thought to be inherently pleasing to the human eye. It is expressed when a line is divided such that the ratio of the whole to the larger part is the same as the larger part to the smaller part.

q: A yellowish, cozy light temperature suited to living rooms and bedrooms is known as what?
o: Warm Light
Ambient Light
Cool Light
Natural Light
n: Warm Light is yellowish and cozy — good for living rooms and bedrooms.

q: A room's focal point can be architectural or decorative. Which choice below is an architectural example?
o: A window with a nice view, or a fireplace
An eye-catching piece of furniture
A striking piece of wall art
A rug with a strong pattern
n: A focal point can be architectural (e.g., a fireplace, a window with a view) or decorative (e.g., bold artwork, statement furniture).

q: How would you define The Modulor?
o: The ratios of a musical scale applied to room dimensions
A mathematical ratio found in nature
A 20th-century attempt by Le Corbusier to reconcile the mathematical beauty of the Golden Section with the physical realities of the human body, based on a man with an arm raised (2.262 meters)
A vernacular modular system evolved from the size of a floor mat
n: The Modulor is a 20th-century attempt to reconcile the mathematical beauty of the Golden Section with the physical realities of the human body. Le Corbusier developed a scale of proportions based on a man with an arm raised (2.262 meters), allowing for a standardized modular system applied from a chair to a city block.

q: Blue, green, and purple read as calming and spacious, making them well suited to bedrooms and baths. What group of colors is this?
o: Primary Colors
Neutral Colors
Cool Colors
Warm Colors
n: Cool Colors (blue, green, purple) are calming, spacious, and relaxing — ideal for bedrooms and bathrooms.

q: How does the source define Harmony in an interior scheme?
o: A space's overall sense of cohesion despite having varied elements
Placing contrasting elements together to sharpen their differences
An appealing combination achieved through things like a unified palette, matching materials, or a shared theme (Scandinavian, Industrial, etc.)
Judging an object's size against a familiar reference point
n: Harmony is a pleasing combination of elements, often achieved through a unified color palette, consistent materials, or thematic elements (e.g., Scandinavian, Industrial).

q: As the source material defines it, SCALE means what?
o: How one part of a composition relates to another, or to the whole
A balanced equilibrium among a design's parts
Signaling a form's importance through its size, shape, or placement
How we judge an object's size against a familiar reference — typically the human body or the space around it
n: Scale is the perception of size. It refers to how we perceive the size of an object in relation to a standard reference, usually the human body or the surrounding environment.

q: Aside from setting a room's mood, what other job can color perform, per the source?
o: It makes natural or artificial lighting unnecessary
It serves no purpose other than decoration
It can direct the eye or break up visual monotony
It fixes a room's temperature permanently
n: Use color to guide focus or break up monotony.

q: A round mirror hung above a rectangular console table demonstrates which kind of contrast?
o: Pattern contrast
Shape contrast
Color contrast
Material contrast
n: Shape contrast is illustrated by a circular mirror above a rectangular console.

q: Meaning that comes from a building's cultural or historical associations is called which kind of architectural character?
o: Functional Character
Symbolic Character
Personal Character
Associated Character
n: Associated Character is the meaning derived from cultural or historical associations.

q: Linen, rattan, and brick fall under which texture category, prized for adding warmth and coziness?
o: Rough/Matte
Tactile only
Visual only
Smooth/Glossy
n: Rough/Matte textures add warmth and coziness (e.g., linen, rattan, brick).

q: When evaluating Functionality, which of these is a question the source recommends asking?
o: What would the furniture resell for?
How many people can legally occupy the room?
Does the room follow the latest trend on social media?
Is there sufficient storage space?
n: When assessing functionality, ask: Is there enough storage? Is it easy to move around? Is lighting adequate for the activities in the space? Are the materials appropriate for the use (e.g., washable fabric in a dining area)? A room should suit its occupants' lifestyle, not just follow trends.

q: How is Positive Space defined in interior design?
o: The empty stretches between and around objects
A slow, incremental shift in design elements
How large an object appears to be
The spots where furniture and decor items sit
n: Positive Space is where objects (furniture, décor) are placed.

q: The source gives placement advice for two texture types — cozy knitted throws and shiny metal or mirror finishes. What does it recommend?
o: Both are meant strictly for bathrooms
The source gives no placement guidance for either
Cozy textures work well in cooler rooms; shiny textures help bounce light into dim ones
Cozy textures belong in sunny, warm rooms; shiny textures only suit cooler spots
n: Use cozy textures (like knitted throws) in cooler areas. Use shiny textures (metal, mirrors) to reflect light in dim spaces.

q: Symmetrical Balance is best described as what?
o: Pairing unlike elements that carry equal visual weight
Arranging elements around a central point
A slow, incremental shift in elements
Splitting elements evenly across a central axis
n: Symmetrical Balance is the equal distribution of elements on both sides of a central axis.

q: Lines that run horizontally — as in beds, tables, and shelves — tend to evoke which quality?
o: Energy, movement, and softness
Calm, stability, and restfulness
Strength, growth, and formality
Drama and emphasis
n: Horizontal Lines, found in beds, tables, and shelves, evoke calm, stability, and restfulness. They are used to widen a space.

q: An organic, flowing pattern with a feminine or traditional feel describes which pattern type?
o: Floral
Ethnic Motifs
Abstract
Geometric
n: Floral patterns are organic and flowing — feminine or traditional.

q: Ching (2014) defines HIERARCHY as what?
o: The perception of size relative to a standard reference
The relationship of one part to another, or to the whole
The juxtaposition of different elements to intensify their individual characteristics
The articulation of the importance of a form or space by its size, shape, or placement
n: Ching, F. D. K. (2014), Architecture: Form, Space, and Order, defines hierarchy as the articulation of the importance of a form or space by its size, shape, or placement.

q: Diagonal, curved, or zigzag lines — Dynamic Lines, often seen in accent furniture or staircases — contribute what to a space?
o: Only structural stability
Rigidity and formality
Coldness and detachment
Playfulness, energy, movement, and softness depending on form
n: Dynamic Lines (diagonal, curved, zigzag) add energy, movement, and softness depending on form. Curves and diagonals add playfulness and are often found in accent furniture or staircases.

q: Broadly speaking, what does Balance aim to achieve in an interior?
o: Keeping a space dramatic and visually lively
Building movement and flow via repeated elements
Spreading elements out evenly so a room feels stable rather than lopsided or chaotic
Turning a good design into an exceptional one through fine details
n: Balance in interior design is about achieving a sense of equilibrium and stability in a room by distributing elements evenly. It ensures the room doesn't feel lopsided or chaotic.

q: How is UNITY defined within a design?
o: Placing contrasting elements together to sharpen their differences
A feeling of oneness where every part of a design belongs together
An object's three-dimensional shape
Judging an object's size against a reference point
n: Unity is the sense of harmony and 'oneness' in a design, where all parts belong together.

q: Irregular, natural forms like curved chairs or oval tables, common in boho, eclectic, or nature-inspired schemes, are known as what?
o: Radial Forms
Organic Forms
Geometric Forms
Tactile Forms
n: Organic Forms are irregular, natural forms (e.g., curved chairs, oval tables), used in boho, eclectic, or nature-inspired interiors.

q: Describe Radial Balance in interior design principles, including what effect it produces.
o: Two identical sofas facing each other — creates calm and predictability
A gradual change in wall colors
Elements arranged around a central point, such as a round dining table with equally spaced chairs or a chandelier surrounded by furniture — draws attention naturally and creates a sense of movement
A large sofa balanced by two smaller chairs — creates a casual look
n: Radial Balance arranges elements around a central point — for example, a round dining table with equally spaced chairs, or a chandelier surrounded by furniture. It draws attention naturally and creates a sense of movement.

q: How does Variety relate to Contrast?
o: How one part relates to another, or to the whole
Bringing in different elements to keep things visually interesting and avoid monotony
A slow, incremental shift in elements
Setting elements close together, especially to invite comparison
n: Variety is the use of different elements to create visual interest and prevent monotony.

q: Light entering through windows and skylights, making a space feel bigger and more welcoming, is what kind of light?
o: Natural Light
Artificial Light
Task Light
Accent Light
n: Natural Light comes from windows and skylights. It makes spaces feel larger and more inviting.

q: Progression, as a rhythm concept (e.g., vases growing steadily larger), is defined how?
o: Two or more elements alternating in sequence
A subtle, smooth flow from one element to another
Gradual changes in elements, such as a series of vases increasing in size or a gradient of wall colors
The use of the same color or pattern across a space
n: Progression is gradual changes in elements — e.g., a series of vases that increase in size, or a gradient of wall colors.

q: Which of the following is NOT among the three benefits Proportion is said to provide?
o: Historically, the chief way of realizing the Vitruvian ideal of Venustas (Delight)
Letting the eye move through a space with a sense of order
Ensuring the building satisfies fire and life-safety codes
Making different parts of a building read as belonging to one family
n: Proportion provides: (1) different parts of a building feel like they belong to the same family; (2) it allows the eye to navigate the space with a sense of order; and (3) historically, it has been the primary vehicle for achieving the Vitruvian ideal of Venustas (Delight).

q: Spotlighting artwork or lighting the underside of cabinets for dramatic emphasis — which artificial-light type is this?
o: Accent Light
Natural Light
Ambient Light
Task Light
n: Accent Light is used for drama and emphasis, such as spotlights on art or under-cabinet lighting.

q: Why does the source say every room needs a focal point (Emphasis)?
o: It gives the eye somewhere to land and anchors the space — without it a room can feel flat, though too many can feel chaotic
It cuts down on the need for artificial lighting
It boosts the room's storage capacity
It keeps the room in step with current trends
n: Every room needs a focal point — something that immediately draws the eye and anchors the space. All other design elements should support, and not distract from, this point. A room without emphasis can feel bland; too many focal points can feel chaotic.

q: Which pair of Renaissance theorists treated architecture as 'frozen music,' mapping musical-scale ratios onto room dimensions?
o: Andrea Palladio and Leon Battista Alberti
Vitruvius and Pevsner
Walter Gropius and Ludwig Mies van der Rohe
Le Corbusier and Le Corbusier's collaborators
n: Renaissance theorists like Andrea Palladio and Leon Battista Alberti believed that architecture was 'frozen music.' They applied the ratios of a musical scale (consonances) to the dimensions of rooms.

q: Red, orange, and yellow — inviting, energizing, but potentially overwhelming in large amounts — describe which color group?
o: Warm Colors
Neutral Colors
Accent Colors
Cool Colors
n: Warm Colors (red, orange, yellow) are inviting and energizing, cozy — but can feel intense in large doses.

q: In an interior-design context, what does Scale actually refer to?
o: The mood a color choice sets
How one part of a whole relates to another part — like a lampshade to its base
How one object's size compares to another's, especially relative to the room — an oversized sectional in a small studio, for instance, throws off scale
A decorative motif that repeats
n: Scale is the relationship between one object's size and another's, especially in relation to the space. For example, an oversized sectional in a small studio disrupts scale. Scale is about spatial awareness and how furniture fits within a room.

q: The Ken, Japan's traditional modular system, is best described how?
o: A ratio that occurs naturally and recurs in nature
A 20th-century system devised by Le Corbusier
A vernacular grid system rooted in the size of a tatami mat and the spacing between columns, flexible enough for both standardized building and varied spatial layouts
Applying musical ratios to a room's dimensions
n: The Ken is a Japanese vernacular modular system that evolved from the size of a floor mat (Tatami) and the distance between columns. It provides a flexible grid that allows for both standardized construction and varied spatial experiences.

q: For a harmonious palette, how many main colors does the source recommend limiting yourself to?
o: 1 color only
As many as possible
2–3 main colors
5–6 main colors
n: Limit your palette to 2–3 main colors for harmony. Light colors expand space; dark colors add depth and coziness.

q: Smooth leather set against rough wood is an example of which type of contrast?
o: Color contrast
Shape contrast
Pattern contrast
Material contrast
n: Material contrast is illustrated by smooth leather vs. rough wood. Without contrast, a room can feel flat; but too much contrast without unity can feel disjointed.

q: A building's appearance, shaped by what it's used for internally, is described by which type of architectural character?
o: Personal Character
Historical Character
Associated Character
Functional Character
n: Functional Character is the appearance of a building derived from its internal use.

q: Define Visual Texture.
o: Texture that is perceived with the eyes, such as a photo of a furry blanket
The emotional tone set by a material
Texture that can be physically felt
A pattern used to energize a space
n: Visual Texture is perceived with the eyes (e.g., a photo of a furry blanket).

q: In interior design, 'Details' — the small choices that push a design from good to exceptional — include which of the following?
o: Things like cushion or curtain trim, cabinet pulls, switch-plate covers, and upholstery stitching
The city's zoning regulations
Only the room's overall floor plan
The building's structural engineering
n: Details are often overlooked, but they elevate a design from good to exceptional. This includes trim on cushions or curtains, cabinet handles, light switch plates, and stitching on upholstery.

q: Within the Principles of Interior Design, how is Space defined as an element?
o: An object's three-dimensional shape
The room's physical footprint — floor area plus height — the surface everything else gets arranged on
A recurring decorative motif meant to energize a space
The visual pathways that guide the eye and shape a room
n: Space refers to the physical area available in a room, both the floor area and the height. It's the canvas where all other elements are placed. Good space planning ensures ease of movement and accessibility.

q: Per the source, what's the reasoning behind mixing different textures in a room?
o: To build depth, since color alone can't carry that job
To do away with needing a color palette altogether
To make a space feel flatter and less layered
To dial back a room's tactile qualities
n: Mix different textures to add depth — don't rely solely on color.

q: Ching (2014) defines BALANCE in architecture as what?
o: Placing unlike elements next to one another
The recurring return of architectural elements
How one part relates to another part, or to the whole
Equilibrium among a design's parts, reached by distributing visual weight across an axis or center point
n: Ching, F. D. K. (2014), Architecture: Form, Space, and Order, defines balance as the state of equilibrium between parts of a design, achieved through the distribution of 'visual weight' across an axis or center point.

q: As an interior design element, how is Line defined?
o: Visual pathways that guide the eye, shaping everything's form and coloring a room's energy
A recurring decorative motif meant to energize and enrich a space
How a material feels or looks on its surface
An object's three-dimensional makeup — height, width, depth
n: Line refers to the visual paths that guide the eye. Lines shape the form of everything and influence the energy of a room.

q: Squares, chevrons, and stripes — modern, structured — belong to which pattern category?
o: Floral
Damask
Abstract
Geometric
n: Geometric patterns (squares, chevrons, stripes) are modern and structured.

q: Ching (2014) defines RHYTHM in architecture as what?
o: The articulation of the importance of a form or space by its size, shape, or placement
The movement characterized by a patterned recurrence of architectural elements, guiding the eye through repetition, alternation, or progression
The comparison of two or more dimensions
The state of equilibrium between parts of a design
n: Ching, F. D. K. (2014), Architecture: Form, Space, and Order, defines rhythm as the movement characterized by a patterned recurrence of architectural elements, guiding the eye through a space using repetition, alternation, or progression.

q: What does the source say happens when a space overuses vertical lines, or overuses horizontal lines?
o: Both produce identical visual effects
Neither line orientation affects a room's feel
Too many verticals can feel playful; too many horizontals, dynamic
Too many verticals can feel stiff; too many horizontals can feel static
n: Too many verticals can feel rigid; too many horizontals may seem static.

q: Which group of patterns is singled out for adding 'character and cultural references'?
o: Geometric and Floral only
Animal Prints, Ethnic Motifs, Damask, and Paisley
None of the pattern types add cultural references
Abstract patterns only
n: Animal Prints, Ethnic Motifs, Damask, and Paisley add character and cultural references.

q: How is Emphasis defined as a hierarchy-related strategy?
o: Comparing two or more dimensions against each other
A vernacular grid system rooted in a floor mat's size
Splitting elements evenly across a central axis
Making one element stand out from the rest, giving the eye a focal point so a design doesn't read as flat or aimless
n: Emphasis is the strategy of making one element stand out among others. It creates a point of interest — often called a 'focal point' — that captures attention and prevents a design from appearing flat or directionless.

q: Clean-edged, manmade forms such as squares and rectangles, common in modern and minimalist design, are called what?
o: Dynamic Forms
Geometric Forms
Tactile Forms
Organic Forms
n: Geometric Forms are clean-edged, manmade forms (e.g., squares, rectangles), often used in modern and minimalist designs.

q: In interior design principles, what does Asymmetrical Balance typically look like?
o: A round table with chairs spaced evenly around it
A large sofa offset by two smaller chairs across from it — a more casual, modern look that takes a practiced eye, since it relies on dynamic tension
Two matching sofas facing one another
A chandelier ringed by furniture
n: Asymmetrical Balance is more casual and modern — for example, a large sofa balanced by two smaller chairs on the opposite side. It requires a trained eye to get right, as it's more dynamic.

q: Define CONTRAST as a design concept.
o: A ratio that recurs naturally in the world
Signaling a form's importance through its size, shape, or placement
Equilibrium among a design's parts
Sharpening the individual qualities of different elements by setting them against each other — through shifts in color, texture, shape, or material
n: Contrast is the juxtaposition of different elements to intensify their individual characteristics. It can be achieved through changes in color, texture, shape, or material.

q: Using a beautiful-but-uncomfortable chair as the example, what does 'maintaining form-function balance' mean?
o: Form and function can never coexist in one object
Even a gorgeous chair still has to be comfortable to sit in
Function must always win out over form
Form must always win out over function
n: Maintaining form-function balance means, for example, that a beautiful chair still needs to be comfortable.

q: Repetition, as a rhythm device — say, blue throw pillows, a blue rug, and blue curtains — is defined how?
o: A smooth, gentle flow from one area to the next
Slow, incremental change across elements
Repeating the same color, shape, or pattern throughout a space
Two or more elements taking turns in sequence
n: Repetition is the use of the same color, shape, or pattern across the space — e.g., blue throw pillows, a blue rug, and blue curtains.

q: PROPORTION is nicknamed 'The Logic of Ratios.' What does it actually refer to?
o: How one part relates to another or to the whole — used to build Harmony, where every part of a building seems to share the same family of shapes
Equilibrium among a design's parts
The expressive traits of a building that let an onlooker read its purpose
The recurring return of architectural elements
n: Proportion, 'The Logic of Ratios,' is the relationship of one part to another, or to the whole. Proportion is used to achieve Harmony, where all parts of a building appear to belong to the same family of shapes — it is inherently about the comparison of two or more dimensions.

q: Reading lamps and kitchen lighting are examples of which artificial-light category, used for specific tasks?
o: Ambient Light
Accent Light
Natural Light
Task Light
n: Task Light is critical for specific activities, such as reading lamps or kitchen lighting.

q: Transition, as a rhythm concept — swapping a doorway for an archway, say — is defined how?
o: A subtle, smooth flow from one space or element to another, such as using an archway instead of a doorway or curved furniture
Two or more elements alternating in sequence
Gradual changes in elements
The use of the same color, shape, or pattern across a space
n: Transition is a subtle, smooth flow from one space or element to another — e.g., using an archway instead of a doorway, or curved furniture. Good rhythm creates flow and a sense of predictability and comfort.

q: Within the Classical Orders, what element functions as the proportional 'Module,' or basic unit?
o: The diameter of the column
The span of the roof
The width of the pediment
The height of the entablature
n: In the Classical tradition, the diameter of the column serves as the 'Module' (basic unit) for the system of proportion.

q: A bluish, clean light temperature well suited to task-heavy areas like kitchens or offices is known as what?
o: Warm Light
Cool Light
Natural Light
Accent Light
n: Cool Light is bluish and clean — great for task-heavy zones like kitchens or offices.

q: Which proportional system, roughly 1:1.618, is commonly applied to achieve natural-feeling proportions — such as a lamp shade sized to its base — in interior design?
o: The Golden Ratio
Renaissance Musical Ratio
The Modulor
The Ken
n: Proportion is the relationship between parts of a whole — for example, a lamp shade that's proportionate to the lamp base. The golden ratio (about 1:1.618) is often used to achieve natural proportions.

q: Standing how tall was the raised-arm figure Le Corbusier used as the basis for the Modulor?
o: 3.05 meters
1.618 meters
1.75 meters
2.262 meters
n: Le Corbusier developed the Modulor as a scale of proportions based on a man with an arm raised at 2.262 meters, allowing for a standardized modular system applied to everything from a chair to a city block.

q: White, gray, beige, and black — timeless, versatile, and able to pair with any palette — describe which color group?
o: Warm Colors
Neutral Colors
Accent Colors
Cool Colors
n: Neutral Colors (white, gray, beige, black) are timeless and versatile — they create balance and work with any palette.

q: In interior design, how is Unity defined, and why does 'variety within unity' matter?
o: Unity is a room's overall cohesion — despite varied elements, it reads as one complete idea; 'variety within unity' keeps things from looking too perfectly matched (and dull) while still holding a sense of order
Unity requires every element to match exactly, with zero variation permitted
Unity has nothing to do with harmony
Unity is only a matter of matching colors
n: Unity is the overall cohesion of the space — despite varying elements, the room feels like a complete idea. Variety within unity is important: you don't want everything to match perfectly (which can be boring), but you want a sense of order and relationship between things.

q: Pevsner (1943), in An Outline of European Architecture, defines Architectural Character as what?
o: A building's expressive traits, which let an onlooker read its purpose, origin, or the designer's intent — the quality making a building look like what it's meant to be
How visual weight is spread across an axis
The mathematical ratio behind a building's proportions
The recurring return of architectural elements
n: Pevsner, N. (1943), An Outline of European Architecture, defines Character as the expressive qualities of a building that allow an observer to identify its purpose, origin, or the intent of the designer. It is the quality that makes a building look like what it is meant to be.

q: Define Tactile Texture.
o: Texture that can be physically felt, such as rough stone or smooth leather
A repeated decorative design
Texture that is perceived only with the eyes, like a photo of a furry blanket
The three-dimensional structure of an object
n: Tactile Texture can be physically felt (e.g., rough stone, smooth leather).

q: Black against white, or light against dark, illustrates which type of contrast?
o: Material contrast
Pattern contrast
Color contrast
Shape contrast
n: Color contrast is illustrated by black and white, or light vs. dark. Contrast adds drama and keeps a space visually exciting.

q: The individual architect's distinctive style is described by which type of architectural character?
o: Associated Character
Modular Character
Functional Character
Personal Character
n: Personal Character is the unique style of the individual architect.

q: Glass, lacquered wood, and tile — modern and clean-feeling — belong to which texture category?
o: Rough/Matte
Tactile only
Smooth/Glossy
Organic
n: Smooth/Glossy textures feel modern and clean (e.g., glass, lacquered wood, tiles). Shiny textures are also used to reflect light in dim spaces.

q: How are design principles in architecture defined?
o: Codes that regulate a building's construction safety
A timeline of architectural movements through history
The core conceptual tools used to arrange architectural elements into a unified, meaningful whole
A roster of licensed architects and their notable works
n: Design principles in architecture are the fundamental conceptual tools used to organize and arrange architectural elements into a cohesive and meaningful whole.

q: What is Negative Space in interior design, and why does it matter?
o: It's the empty space around and between objects, valuable for giving a room breathing room, avoiding clutter, and letting focal points stand out
It's where furniture sits, and it matters for setting the color palette
It's a room's ceiling height, which matters for acoustics
It's a type of dynamic line found in staircases
n: Negative Space is the empty area around and between objects — important for creating breathing room. Negative space helps avoid clutter and makes focal points stand out.

q: As an interior design element, how is Pattern defined?
o: An object's three-dimensional makeup
The physical footprint available in a room
A recurring decorative motif meant to energize and enrich a space
How a material feels on its surface
n: A pattern is a repeated decorative design used to energize and enhance a space.

q: Give a definition of Asymmetrical Balance.
o: Placing contrasting elements together to sharpen their differences
Splitting elements evenly across a central axis
Arranging elements around a central point
Combining unlike elements that carry equal visual weight
n: Asymmetrical Balance is the use of dissimilar elements that have equal visual weight.

q: What do Vertical Lines — as seen in doorways, curtains, or tall cabinets — tend to suggest?
o: Strength, growth, and formality
Coziness and warmth
Playfulness and energy
Calm, stability, and restfulness
n: Vertical Lines, seen in doorways, curtains, and tall cabinets, suggest strength, growth, and formality. They are used to draw the eye upward, though too many verticals can feel rigid.

q: Which pattern type is characterized as 'expressive and creative'?
o: Damask
Geometric
Abstract
Floral
n: Abstract patterns are expressive and creative.

q: How does Unwin (2013), in Analysing Architecture, further define hierarchy?
o: As the articulation of the importance or significance of a form or space by its size, shape, or placement relative to the other forms and spaces of the organization
As the sense of harmony and 'oneness' in a design
As the state of being placed close together for comparison
As a mathematical ratio found in nature
n: Unwin, S. (2013), Analysing Architecture, describes hierarchy as the articulation of the importance or significance of a form or space by its size, shape, or placement relative to the other forms and spaces of the organization.

q: As an interior design element, how is Form defined?
o: The visual paths that guide the eye
The physical area available in a room
The surface feel or visual appearance of a material
The three-dimensional structure of an object — height, width, and depth
n: Form is the three-dimensional structure of an object — height, width, and depth.

q: In interior design principles, what does Symmetrical Balance look like, and what feeling does it produce?
o: A large sofa balanced by two smaller chairs; creates a dynamic look
A round dining table with equally spaced chairs; creates movement
A chandelier surrounded by furniture; draws attention naturally
Two identical sofas facing each other with a coffee table in between; traditional and formal, creating calm, order, and predictability
n: Symmetrical Balance is traditional and formal — for example, two identical sofas facing each other with a coffee table in between. It creates calm, order, and predictability.

q: Fill in Ching's definition (Architecture: Form, Space, and Order): 'Unity is the state of being combined or at one... it suggests that the elements of a design are tied together by a commonality of some kind, so that they appear to belong to the ___.'
o: same building
same family
same era
same architect

q: Using a square table paired with round chairs as the example, what does 'mixing forms' achieve in interior design?
o: It always undermines form-function balance
It introduces variety and can work very well
It removes the need for negative space
It's only relevant in outdoor landscaping
n: Mixing forms creates variety. A square table with round chairs can be very effective.

q: Broadly, what purpose does Rhythm serve in an interior?
o: It is the relationship between one part of a room and another
It achieves equilibrium and stability by distributing elements evenly
It guides the eye through a room and keeps the visual experience interesting
It refers only to a room's color palette
n: Rhythm guides the eye through a room and keeps the visual experience interesting.
